messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF at S1).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 0.76 V at S1; compare it with the
output window and the diode drops.
  S1: nominal (weak); Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 6800 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weakest excitation; Ip = 8 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 22000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 10 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 12 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 10000 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       0.56   0.566    11.6       -    0.0314  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S2      0.558   0.563    11.2       -    0.0457  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       2.24    2.26    35.4   0.329     0.228  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S4      0.334   0.339    8.95       -   0.00508  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S5      0.573   0.581    15.7       -    0.0329  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S6      0.459   0.462     6.1       -    0.0211  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Input: Piezoelectric transducer (sinusoidal current source $I_p$, capacitance $C_p$, leakage $20\text{ M}\Omega$).
    *   Output: Load $R_L$ from node "out".
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{ V}$ (settled mean)
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{ V}$ (absolute max)
        *   $\text{ripple } V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{ V}$ (final window)
        *   $\text{startup } t_{up} \le 0.4\text{ s}$ (time to reach $1.8\text{ V}$)
        *   $\text{settled } dv \le 0.02\text{ V}$ (stability between last two windows)
    *   Piezo Model:
        *   S1 (Nominal): $I_p=12\mu\text{A}$, $f=100\text{ Hz}$, $C_p=25\text{ nF}$, $R_L=10\text{ M}\Omega$.
        *   $V_{oc} = \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p} \approx \frac{12\mu\text{A}}{2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 0.76\text{ V}$.
    *   The $V_{oc}$ is very low (0.76 V). A standard bridge rectifier (FBR) fails because the diode drops (DSCH $\sim 0.25\text{ V} \times 2 = 0.5\text{ V}$) leave very little voltage for the load, and more importantly, the piezo voltage amplitude (0.76 V) is barely above the threshold for conducting.

    *   Passive Rectification (FBR): Already tested, fails. $V_{oc}$ is too low to overcome diode drops and reach 1.8 V.
    *   Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) or Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI):
        *   SSHI uses an inductor and a switch to invert the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the voltage across the rectifier.
        *   SECE is similar but typically uses a switch to disconnect the piezo and dump charge into a storage cap.
    *   Since $V_{oc}$ is only $\sim 0.76\text{ V}$, we definitely need a boost mechanism. A standard SSHI (inductor-based voltage inversion) is the classic solution for low $V_{oc}$ piezos.

    *   *Topology A: SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor).*
        *   The piezo is connected to a rectifier.
        *   At the voltage peaks of $C_p$, a switch closes to connect $C_p$ to an inductor $L$, causing an LC oscillation that flips the voltage polarity.
        *   This increases the effective voltage amplitude seen by the rectifier.
        *   Standard SSHI: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Storage Cap. Switch/Inductor flips $C_p$.
        *   Wait, a simpler version of "Synchronous Switching" is the "Parallel-SSHI".
        *   Actually, the most effective for very low voltages is a "Synchronous Switch" that flips the voltage *before* the rectifier.
        *   But if $V_{oc} = 0.76\text{ V}$, and we need $V_{out} = 1.8\text{ V}$, we need a multiplier effect.

    *   *Topology B: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).*
        *   Piezo charges $C_p$ in open circuit.
        *   At the peak, a switch connects $C_p$ to the storage capacitor through a diode.
        *   This can act as a charge pump.

    *   *Topology C: Inductive Boost / Synchronous Rectification.*
        *   If we use a SYNC controller and a switch, we can essentially create a switching converter.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Parallel)**
        *   Piezo ($pzp, pzn$) $\to$ Rectifier (DSCH) $\to$ Storage Cap.
        *   An inductor $L$ and a switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo to flip the voltage.
        *   Wait, the provided components are limited. $L$ is available, $S$ is available (ctrl by SYNC).
        *   Let's refine SSHI:
            *   Piezo nodes: $pzp, pzn$.
            *   Rectifier: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$. (Standard FBR).
            *   Flipping circuit: Switch $S$ and inductor $L$ in parallel with the piezo.
            *   $S$ closes at peaks.
            *   This increases the voltage amplitude across the bridge.

    *   **Design 2: SECE (Simplified)**
        *   The piezo charges $C_p$.
        *   A switch $S$ closes at the peak, dumping charge through a diode $D$ into $C_{out}$.
        *   Since we have $pzp$ and $pzn$, we can use two switches and two diodes for both half-cycles.
        *   S1 (ctrl G1, edges pos): $pzp \to D_1 \to out$.
        *   S2 (ctrl G2, edges neg): $pzn \to D_2 \to out$.
        *   But SECE usually requires an inductor for efficiency or a specific timing.

    *   **Design 3: Inductive Boost / Flyback-ish (Simplified)**
        *   Since we have $S$ and $L$ and $SYNC$, we can try a design where the inductor stores energy.
        *   Piezo $\to$ $L$ $\to$ $S$ (to ground). When $S$ opens, $L$ kicks voltage up.
        *   However, for piezo energy harvesting, the LC-flip (SSHI) is the standard.

    *   *Circuit:*
        *   Diodes: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$ (FBR).
        *   Inductor $L_1$ between $pzp$ and node $n1$.
        *   Switch $S_1$ between $n1$ and $pzn$.
        *   SYNC $G_1$: `edges="both"`, `ton` small (around $30-50 \mu\text{s}$ for $L=4.7\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF} \to \pi\sqrt{LC} \approx 34 \mu\text{s}$), `phase=0`.
        *   Storage Cap $C_{out}$ at `out`.
    *   *Mechanism:* The FBR collects energy. The $L-S$ combination flips the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks, effectively doubling (or more) the voltage range and reducing the effect of diode drops relative to the piezo energy.

    *   *Is there a more efficient way?*
        *   The "Standard SSHI" actually places the flip switch *across* the piezo.
        *   $pzp \to L \to S \to pzn$.
        *   The bridge is still there.
        *   Let's check the reference design again. FBR failed because $V_{oc}$ was too low.
        *   With SSHI, $V_{pzp}$ will swing from $-V_{peak}$ to $+V_{peak}$ and then get flipped, potentially increasing the voltage to $V_{out}$ levels.

    *   Wait, a better SSHI topology for low $V_{oc}$ is to put the rectifier *after* the flipping.
    *   Actually, if $V_{oc} = 0.76\text{ V}$, the voltage across the piezo $C_p$ is $0.76 \sin(\omega t)$.
    *   The bridge rectifier diodes (DSCH) have a drop of $\sim 0.25\text{ V}$.
    *   The voltage reaching $C_{out}$ is $0.76 - 0.5 = 0.26\text{ V}$ (too low).
    *   If we use SSHI, the voltage across $C_p$ is flipped. This doesn't change the *peak* voltage unless the flipping happens at the right time to "pump" the voltage.
    *   Correction: SSHI doesn't just flip; it allows the piezo to maintain a higher average voltage across its terminals, which in turn increases the power extracted. The voltage across $C_p$ can reach values higher than $V_{oc}$.

    *   S1 (Nominal): $P_{load} = V^2/R_L = 1.8^2 / 10\text{M} = 0.324 \mu\text{W}$.
    *   S4 (Weakest): $P_{load} = 1.8^2 / 22\text{M} = 0.147 \mu\text{W}$.
    *   Piezo power: $P_{avg} \approx \frac{1}{2} I_p V_{oc} \approx 0.5 \cdot 12\mu\text{A} \cdot 0.76\text{V} \approx 4.5 \mu\text{W}$ (theoretical max).
    *   The available power is plenty, but the *voltage* is the problem.

    *   *Design 1: SSHI.*
        *   L1: $pzp \to n1$
        *   S1: $n1 \to pzn$
        *   G1: `ton=3e-5, edges="both", phase=0`
        *   Bridge: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$
        *   Storage: $C_1(out, 0)$

    *   *Design 2: SECE (Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction).*
        *   In SECE, the piezo is not connected to the load during the cycle.
        *   At the peak, the charge is extracted.
        *   $S_1(pzp, n1), S_2(pzn, n2)$
        *   $D_1(n1, out), D_2(n2, out)$
        *   $C_1(out, 0)$
        *   $G_1(\text{pos}), G_2(\text{neg})$
        *   Wait, without an inductor, this is just a switch-capacitor. To get $1.8\text{ V}$ from $0.76\text{ V}$, we need to accumulate charge.
        *   If we use the inductor in the extraction path (Inductive SECE), it's much more efficient.
        *   $pzp \to S_1 \to L \to D_1 \to out$.

    *   *Design 3: A Charge Pump (Voltage Doubler) variant.*
        *   Since the frequency is low (100 Hz), we can use a SYNC controller to implement a switched-capacitor pump.
        *   $S_1(pzp, n1)$, $C_{pump}(n1, n2)$, $S_2(n2, out)$.
        *   This is likely too complex for 16 components.

    *   SSHI is the most robust choice for piezo energy harvesting.
    *   Let's refine the SSHI connectivity.
    *   $pzp \to L \to S \to pzn$ is the flip.
    *   The FBR is $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$.
    *   Wait, if $S$ is across the piezo, the bridge diodes will still be there.
    *   Is there a better way to use the SYNC?
    *   If we use a SYNC to simply act as a synchronous rectifier (replacing the diodes), we'd need 4 switches. We only have 4 switches total.
    *   Let's try:
        1. SSHI (FBR + Inductor Flip)
        2. SECE (Inductor-based extraction)
        3. A simpler "Boost" using the piezo as a source for an inductive boost converter.

    *   Wait, I can use the SYNC to implement a "Synchronous Rectifier" for one half-cycle and a diode for the other? No, too complex.
    *   Let's focus on SSHI. The critical part is the LC resonance $\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.
    *   $C_p = 25\text{ nF}, L = 10\text{ mH} \to \pi\sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 50 \mu\text{s}$.
    *   $L = 4.7\text{ mH} \to \pi\sqrt{4.7\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx 34 \mu\text{s}$.

    *   *Alternative for Design 2: SECE.*
        *   $pzp \to S_1 \to n1$.
        *   $pzn \to S_2 \to n2$.
        *   $n1 \to L \to D_1 \to out$.
        *   $n2 \to L \to D_2 \to out$.
        *   No, that's too many inductors.
        *   One inductor: $S_1(pzp, n1), S_2(pzn, n1), n1 \to L \to D \to out$.
        *   $G_1(\text{pos}), G_2(\text{neg})$.

    *   *Refining SSHI again:*
        *   Components: 4 Diodes (Bridge), 1 Inductor, 1 Switch, 1 SYNC, 1 Cap. (Total 8).
        *   This is well within the 16-component limit.

    *   *Wait, check the "Reference Design" again.*
        *   The FBR failed. SSHI is the logical next step.
        *   Another option is a "Voltage Doubler" (Dickson charge pump), but that requires a higher AC voltage than we have.

    *   *One more check on SSHI:*
        *   $S$ closes at $V_{pzp} = V_{peak}$.
        *   Current flows $pzp \to L \to S \to pzn$.
        *   $L$ charges. Then $S$ opens.
        *   $V_{pzp}$ flips to $\approx -V_{peak}$.
        *   This happens every half cycle.
        *   The bridge rectifier then converts this to DC.
        *   The key is that the flip increases the voltage across the piezo, and the diodes now see a larger voltage, making the 0.5 V drop less significant.

    *   Design 1: `sshi_fbr`
        *   FBR: `D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)`
        *   Flip: `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn), G1(ton=3e-5, edges="both", phase=0)`
        *   Cap: `C1(out, 0)`
    *   Design 2: `sece_inductive`
        *   Extraction: `S1(pzp, n1), G1(edges="pos"), S2(pzn, n1), G2(edges="neg")`
        *   Boost: `L1(n1, n2), D1(n2, out), C1(out, 0)`
        *   Wait, SECE usually has a capacitor and a switch. Let's try: `S1(pzp, n1), G1(pos), D1(n1, out), C1(out, 0)`. But that's just a diode. The inductor is key.
        *   Let's try a simpler version: `S1(pzp, n1), G1(pos), L1(n1, n2), D1(n2, out), C1(out, 0)`. And for the other side: `S2(pzn, n1), G2(neg)`.
    *   Design 3: `boost_converter`
        *   Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ Boost Converter.
        *   FBR $\to$ $C_{mid} \to$ $L_{boost} \to S_{boost} \to 0$.
        *   $L_{boost} \to D_{boost} \to out$.
        *   This is basically an FBR followed by a DC-DC boost.
        *   $S_{boost}$ controlled by SYNC.
        *   Wait, SYNC tracks the *piezo* frequency, not a DC-DC clock. So the boost would run at 100 Hz (or 200 Hz).
        *   $L_{boost}$ would need to be quite large.

    *   Let's stick to SSHI and SECE as they are the industry standards for this.

    *   Actually, I'll propose:
        1.  SSHI with FBR (the most likely candidate).
        2.  SSHI with a simpler Half-Wave Rectifier (to see if it helps).
        3.  Inductive SECE.

    *   Wait, the SSHI flip is usually performed with a switch and inductor *in parallel* with the piezo.
    *   $pzp \to L \to S \to pzn$.
    *   And the rectifier is also in parallel.
    *   Let's ensure the `ton` and `phase` are reasonable.
    *   `ton` $\approx 34 \mu\text{s}$ for $L=4.7\text{mH}$.
    *   `phase` should be $0$ to trigger at the peaks.

    *   S1: $I_p=12\mu\text{A}, f=100, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=10\text{M} \to V_{out} \ge 1.8\text{V}$.
    *   S4: $I_p=8\mu\text{A}, f=100, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=22\text{M} \to V_{out} \ge 1.8\text{V}$.
    *   S3: $I_p=40\mu\text{A}, f=100, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=22\text{M} \to V_{out} \le 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   The zener `DZ33` could be useful for $V_{out\_max}$. Let's add it as a safety clamp in case the boost is too strong.

    *   `D1(pzp, out), D2(pzn, out), D3(0, pzp), D4(0, pzn)`
    *   `L1(pzp, n1), S1(n1, pzn), G1(ton=3e-5, edges="both", phase=0)`
    *   `C1(out, 0)`
    *   `D5(0, out)` model `DZ33` (Zener clamp)

    *   *Self-Correction on SECE:*
        *   SECE is often more efficient than SSHI for very low voltages.
        *   `S1(pzp, n1), G1(edges="pos"), S2(pzn, n1), G2(edges="neg"), L1(n1, n2), D1(n2, out), C1(out, 0)`.
        *   This takes the peak voltage, dumps it into $L$, then $L$ kicks it up to $V_{out}$.
